plain_english: Now we come to a part of this topic that naturally makes us sad and worried. I'm talking about when good men meet terrible ends. When Socrates is forced to die in prison, when Rutilius has to live in exile, when Pompeius and Cicero have to offer their necks to the swords of their own followers, when the great Cato — that living picture of virtue — falls on his sword and destroys both himself and the republic. You can't help feeling grief that Fortune hands out her rewards so unfairly. What hope can a good man have when he sees the best people meeting the worst fates?
original_excerpt: There comes now a part of our subject which is wont with good cause to make one sad and anxious: I mean when good men come to bad ends; when Socrates is forced to die in prison, Rutilius to live in exile, Pompeius and Cicero to offer their necks to the swords of their own followers, when the great Cato, that living image of virtue, falls upon his sword and rips up both himself and the republic, one cannot help being grieved that Fortune should bestow her gifts so unjustly: what, too, can a good man hope to obtain when he sees the best of men meeting with the worst fates.

plain_english: But look at how each of them faced their fate. If they endured it bravely, then long for courage as great as theirs. If they died in a weak and cowardly way, nothing was lost. Either they earned your admiration for their courage, or they showed you exactly the kind of cowardice you shouldn't copy. After all, what could be more shameful than great men dying so bravely that it makes other people into cowards?
original_excerpt: Well, but see how each of them endured his fate, and if they endured it bravely, long in your heart for courage as great as theirs; if they died in a womanish and cowardly manner, nothing was lost: either they deserved that you should admire their courage, or else they did not deserve that you should wish to imitate their cowardice: for what can be more shameful than that the greatest men should die so bravely as to make people cowards.

plain_english: Let us praise someone who deserves endless praise, and say, 'The braver you are, the happier you are! You have escaped all accidents, jealousy, and disease. You have escaped from prison. The gods didn't think you deserved misfortune — they decided that fortune no longer deserved any power over you.' But when someone pulls back at the moment of death and looks longingly at life, we must take hold of them.
original_excerpt: Let us praise one who deserves such constant praises, and say, "The braver you are the happier you are! You have escaped from all accidents, jealousies, diseases: you have escaped from prison: the gods have not thought you worthy of ill-fortune, but have thought that fortune no longer deserved to have any power over you": but when any one shrinks back in the hour of death and looks longingly at life, we must lay hands upon him.

plain_english: I will never cry for a man who dies happily, or for one who dies crying. The cheerful one dries my tears. The weeping one makes himself unworthy of anyone's tears. Should I weep for Hercules because he was burned alive? Or for Regulus because he was pierced by so many nails? Or for Cato because he reopened his wounds a second time? All these men figured out how to trade a small bit of time for immortality. Through their deaths, they gained eternal life.
original_excerpt: I will never weep for a man who dies cheerfully, nor for one who dies weeping: the former wipes away my tears, the latter by his tears makes himself unworthy that any should be shed for him. Shall I weep for Hercules because he was burned alive, or for Regulus because he was pierced by so many nails, or for Cato because he tore open his wounds a second time? All these men discovered how at the cost of a small portion of time they might obtain immortality, and by their deaths gained eternal life.
